questions.q: What is the "double coincidence of wants" in a barter system?
questions.a: It is when two people each have something the other person wants, allowing them to trade directly. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks it just means "two people wanting to buy something," missing the requirement that they must also have something the other person desires.

questions.q: If a farmer has rice and wants a pot, but the potter only wants cloth, why does the barter fail?
questions.a: The barter fails because there is no double coincidence of wants; the potter does not want the farmer's rice. A wrong answer indicates the student hasn't grasped that trade requires a mutual match of both the item offered and the item sought.

questions.q: You have a bag of wheat and need a haircut. The barber needs wheat but doesn't have time to cut your hair today. Can you barter? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, you cannot barter because the "want" is not occurring at the same time (coincidence). A wrong answer suggests the student thinks having the item is enough, ignoring the "coincidence" (timing and willingness) aspect.

questions.q: Compare a barter system with a modern market using money. Why is the double coincidence a "flaw"?
questions.a: It is a flaw because it forces people to spend hours searching for the right trading partner instead of focusing on their work. A wrong answer shows the student views barter as just as efficient as money, failing to see the search-cost barrier.

questions.q: Is it possible for a barter trade to happen if only one person wants what the other has? Justify your answer.
questions.a: No, it is not possible because trade is a two-way agreement; if one person refuses, the deal collapses. A wrong answer reveals a misunderstanding of the "coincidence" part of the concept, which implies a mutual (double) agreement.

questions.q: Create a scenario where three people (Farmer, Weaver, Potter) successfully complete a trade using indirect barter.
questions.a: The Farmer gives rice to the Weaver, the Weaver gives cloth to the Potter, and the Potter gives a pot to the Farmer. A poor answer fails to connect all three parties, suggesting the student is struggling to visualize the chain of trades required to overcome the lack of a double coincidence.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Double coincidence of wants is a situation in a barter system where two people must ______ desire exactly what the other person is offering to trade.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you have a basket of fresh ______ and you really want a cricket bat.
What is Double coincidence of wants? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Double coincidence of wants is a situation in a barter system where two people must simultaneously desire exactly what the other person is offering to trade.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Double coincidence of wants?
questions.a: Students often think that if two people have valuable items, a trade *must* happen.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to identify whether a given trade scenario is successful or unsuccessful based on the presence of a double coincidence and explain why a trade fails if it is absent.
